items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-21
items.q: My mother is Victoria D'Neena and out of that marriage came six children.

ctx.x: Now just tell the people who you are. This is the voice of Dominic James LaRocca, better known as Nick LaRocca, leader and manager of the world's first jazz band, known as the creators of jazz. I'll tell you about my early life in music and contact. I was born in 1889 in the city of New Orleans. My father's name was Geronimo LaRocca, who was a trumpet player like myself. My mother is Victoria D'Neena and out of that marriage came six children. I'll give you them in order. Rosario was the oldest. Antonia was my…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-05-21
items.q: The interviewee mentions 'VBD' only in the context of the interviewer reading a letter signed by 'MC' (likely VBD's initials or a pseudonym used in the letter), with no personal interaction or relationship described by the interviewee.

ctx.x: Fair play. From this you can see how well-known this music was in New Orleans. I'll tell you one thing, it didn't even exist in New Orleans at this time. No one played in New Orleans. They had no jazz bands in New Orleans. Mr. Oikwa, would you read that second letter? Okay.

Ragtime jazz and operatic music. New Orleans, Louisiana, June 29, 1918. To the editor of the Times, Picayune. Oh, ho, so our good friend VBD is a muse. So are we. Yes, operatic music is an educated taste. Jazz hasn't even got educating qualities in it. To admire classical music does not indicate one is extremely intelligent. It only indicates you've got some brains. But it does take extreme intelligence and study to appreciate operatic music. Yes, ignoramuses and giants may acquire taste, but music has come down…
We'll see you next time. We'll see you next time. Oh, that was fun.
